sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Kubernetes in the cloud is the managed deployment of the open-source container orchestrator on AWS (EKS), Google Cloud (GKE), or Azure (AKS), where the provider runs the control plane and you operate node pools, ingress, autoscaling, and service mesh on top.
Kubernetes began inside Google as Borg, the system that ran essentially every Google service from 2004 onward. Google open-sourced a redesigned successor in 2014, and by 2018 Kubernetes had decisively won the orchestrator war against Docker Swarm and Apache Mesos. A Kubernetes cluster splits responsibilities into a control plane (the API server, scheduler, controller manager, etcd) and a set of worker nodes that run your containers in Pods. The control plane makes global decisions — what runs where, what to restart, when to scale — while each node runs a kubelet that reports back and a kube-proxy that wires networking. Running this yourself on bare metal is genuinely hard: etcd quorum is fragile, API server certificate rotation is error-prone, and a botched upgrade can take down the whole cluster. This is exactly the pain that managed Kubernetes — EKS, GKE, AKS — was built to eliminate.

Managed Kubernetes means the cloud provider operates the control plane for you. AWS EKS charges roughly $0.10 per hour per cluster for the control plane, runs it across multiple Availability Zones, handles etcd backups, and exposes an API endpoint you authenticate to. GKE and AKS go further and offer a free tier for the control plane, and GKE's Autopilot mode even manages the nodes themselves, leaving you with nothing but Pods to declare. The trade-off for offloading the control plane is twofold: you pay a per-cluster tax (EKS's $73/month is non-trivial at fleet scale), and you accept the provider's upgrade cadence — EKS forces version retirement roughly 14 months after release, so you must keep up. Pokémon Go's launch in July 2016 ran on Google Container Engine (the predecessor name for GKE); Niantic scaled from a pre-launch cluster to thousands of nodes processing millions of player location updates per second, and the managed control plane was critical because their team had no time to operate one themselves while fighting the load.

Node pools are how managed K8s organizes the worker fleet. A node pool is a homogeneous set of VMs — same instance type, same disk, same Kubernetes version — managed as an autoscaling group. You typically run multiple node pools: one of cheap spot instances for stateless batch workers, one of on-demand instances for stateful workloads that cannot be interrupted, one of GPU instances for inference, one of memory-optimized instances for caches. GKE's cluster autoscaler watches for Pending Pods (Pods the scheduler cannot place because no node has enough CPU or memory) and calls the cloud API to add nodes; when nodes are underutilized, it drains and removes them. Slack runs its production workloads on EKS with multiple node pools partitioned by latency sensitivity — interactive API calls go to on-demand pools, while background jobs like message search indexing run on spot pools that tolerate eviction. The cluster autoscaler is the link between the Kubernetes scheduler and the cloud's own autoscaling groups, and tuning its `--scale-down-delay` and `--max-node-provision-time` parameters is a recurring operational task.

Ingress controllers are the layer that turns Kubernetes Services into externally reachable HTTP endpoints. The default `Service` of type `ClusterIP` is only reachable inside the cluster; `NodePort` exposes a port on every node; `LoadBalancer` provisions a cloud TCP load balancer per service, which gets expensive fast. The Ingress resource is the abstraction that lets one cloud load balancer route to many services based on host and path — nginx-ingress, Traefik, and the AWS Load Balancer Controller are popular implementations. On EKS, the AWS Load Balancer Controller can provision an ALB per Ingress, integrating with WAF, ACM certificates, and Shield. Shopify, which migrated its massive Rails monolith onto GKE beginning in 2017, uses an in-house ingress layer in front of GKE's own to handle the millions of Shopify storefronts; the ability to declaratively manage routing rules as Kubernetes Ingress objects made it possible to version and roll back changes through their GitOps pipeline.

Service mesh integration is the next layer beyond Ingress. A service mesh like Istio, Linkerd, or AWS App Mesh gives you mTLS between Pods, traffic shifting for canary deploys, retries, timeouts, and circuit breaking — all configured declaratively without touching application code. The mesh works by injecting a sidecar container (Envoy in Istio's case) into every Pod and intercepting all inbound and outbound traffic. The trade-off is real: sidecars add 5–15ms of latency per hop, consume 100–300MB of RAM per Pod, and materially complicate debugging because traffic now flows through an invisible layer. The newer sidecar-less meshes (Istio Ambient, Cilium Service Mesh) use eBPF or a per-node proxy to reduce this overhead, and managed offerings like GKE's Dataplane V2 and AWS App Mesh hide operational complexity. Slack's migration to a service mesh on EKS let them enforce mTLS across hundreds of internal services without code changes, but they publicly noted the operational learning curve was steep.

The economics and reliability of managed Kubernetes are what make it the default choice for medium and large deployments. Compared to running the same workloads on raw EC2, EKS typically costs 10–30% more once you factor in the control plane fee, higher node overhead for system components, and the operational headcount needed to manage Helm charts, RBAC, and observability — but it pays back in deployment velocity, multi-AZ resilience, and the ecosystem of operators for databases, message queues, and ML workloads. Compared to serverless, K8s offers predictable cost at high steady-state load and avoids cold-start latency, but it is overkill for a single microservice. The right pattern today is a portfolio: serverless functions for event-driven workloads, managed Kubernetes for the bulk of stateless services, managed databases for state, and spot-backed node pools for the cost-sensitive batch tier. Real-world examples reinforce this: Pokémon Go on GKE, Shopify on GKE, Slack on EKS, Stripe on a mix of GKE and ECS, Pinterest on EKS — the trajectory is clear, and managed Kubernetes is the de facto substrate for cloud-era application platforms.

Istio / App Mesh] -.->|sidecar inject| P1 SM -.->|sidecar inject| P3 ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +--------------------------------------------------------------------+ | Managed Control Plane (EKS/GKE/AKS) | | +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ +-------------+ | | | apiserver |---| scheduler |---| ctrl-mgr |---| etcd (HA) | | | +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ +-------------+ | | ^ (provider-operated) | | | authn/authz (IAM <--> RBAC) | +---------|----------------------------------------------------------+ | watch / list +------+--------+ +----------------+ +---------------+ | Node Pool A | | Node Pool B | | Node Pool C | | on-demand | | spot | | GPU | | m5.2xlarge | | m5.4xlarge | | g4dn.xlarge | | | | | | | | [Pod][Pod] | | [Pod][Pod][Pod]| | [Pod infer] | | api api | | worker x3 | | ml-svc | +---------------+ +----------------+ +---------------+ ^ ^ ^ | | | +------+--------+ +----------------+ +---------------+ | Cluster | <-- watches Pending Pods, calls cloud API | | Autoscaler | to add/remove nodes per pool | +---------------+ | | +---------------------+ route by host/path | | Ingress (ALB) |----> api-svc | | AWS LB Controller |----> worker-svc | +---------------------+ | | +---------------------+ mTLS, retries, canary | | Service Mesh |----> sidecar injected into every Pod | | Istio / App Mesh | | +---------------------+ | ``` ### Walkthrough 1. The cloud provider operates the control plane (API server, scheduler, controller manager, etcd) across multiple AZs; you authenticate via cloud IAM mapped to Kubernetes RBAC. 2. You declare workloads as Deployments with Pod specs (CPU/memory requests, node selectors, tolerations); the scheduler places Pods onto nodes in the appropriate node pool. 3. When Pods go Pending because no node has capacity, the Cluster Autoscaler calls the cloud provider's API to provision additional nodes from the matching pool; underused nodes are drained and removed. 4. Ingress controllers (ALB, nginx) translate Ingress resources into cloud load balancers that route external traffic to Services, while an optional service mesh injects sidecars for mTLS and traffic shaping.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- A managed node group: same instance type, same kubelet version.
- EKS/GKE/AKS style: managed control plane + node pools + CA.
- CA watches Pending pods and grows pools to satisfy them.
- K8s_cloud_deploy.py - runnable mock of managed Kubernetes deployment.
- Models: Deployment object -> Pod scheduling on node pools,
- Cluster autoscaler reacting to Pending Pods, and ingress routing.
- Provider always bootstraps min_nodes for HA
- Scale-down: remove underused nodes (skip min_nodes)

**Defines:** `PodSpec`, `Pod`, `Node`, `NodePool`, `ManagedCluster`

```python
# k8s_cloud_deploy.py - runnable mock of managed Kubernetes deployment.
# Models: Deployment object -> Pod scheduling on node pools,
# cluster autoscaler reacting to Pending Pods, and ingress routing.
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import List, Dict, Optional
import json, time, uuid

@dataclass
class PodSpec:
    name: str
    image: str
    cpu_milli: int          # millicores, e.g. 500 = 0.5 vCPU
    mem_mib: int
    node_selector: str = "on-demand"   # on-demand | spot | gpu
    needs_gpu: bool = False

@dataclass
class Pod:
    spec: PodSpec
    node: Optional[str] = None
    phase: str = "Pending"  # Pending -> Running -> Terminating

@dataclass
class Node:
    name: str
    pool: str
    cpu_alloc: int          # millicores
    mem_alloc: int          # MiB
    gpu: int = 0
    cpu_used: int = 0
    mem_used: int = 0
    gpu_used: int = 0
    pods: List[Pod] = field(default_factory=list)

class NodePool:
    """A managed node group: same instance type, same kubelet version."""
    def __init__(self, name: str, pool_type: str,
                 cpu_per_node: int, mem_per_node: int, gpu: int = 0):
        self.name = name
        self.pool_type = pool_type
        self.cpu_per_node = cpu_per_node
        self.mem_per_node = mem_per_node
        self.gpu_per_node = gpu
        self.nodes: List[Node] = []
        self.min_nodes = 2
        self.max_nodes = 50

    def provision(self) -> Node:
        n = Node(f"{self.name}-{len(self.nodes)}",
                 self.pool_type, self.cpu_per_node,
                 self.mem_per_node, self.gpu_per_node)
        self.nodes.append(n)
        print(f"[pool:{self.name}] provisioned node {n.name} "
              f"(cpu={self.cpu_per_node}m mem={self.mem_per_node}MiB)")
        return n

    def fits(self, pod: PodSpec) -> bool:
        if pod.node_selector != self.pool_type:
            return False
        if pod.needs_gpu and self.gpu_per_node == 0:
            return False
        return True

class ManagedCluster:
    """EKS/GKE/AKS style: managed control plane + node pools + CA."""
    def __init__(self, name: str, provider: str):
        self.name = name
        self.provider = provider
        self.pools: Dict[str, NodePool] = {}
        self.deployments: Dict[str, List[Pod]] = {}

    def add_pool(self, pool: NodePool):
        self.pools[pool.name] = pool
        # Provider always bootstraps min_nodes for HA
        for _ in range(pool.min_nodes):
            pool.provision()

    def apply_deployment(self, dep_name: str,
                        spec: PodSpec, replicas: int):
        pods = [Pod(spec=spec) for _ in range(replicas)]
        self.deployments[dep_name] = pods
        print(f"[deploy] {dep_name}: {replicas} replicas of "
              f"{spec.image} (cpu={spec.cpu_milli}m)")
        self._schedule()

    def _schedule(self):
        for dep, pods in self.deployments.items():
            for pod in pods:
                if pod.phase != "Pending":
                    continue
                placed = False
                for pool in self.pools.values():
                    if not pool.fits(pod.spec):
                        continue
                    for node in pool.nodes:
                        if (node.cpu_used + pod.spec.cpu_milli <= node.cpu_alloc
                                and node.mem_used + pod.spec.mem_mib <= node.mem_alloc
                                and (not pod.spec.needs_gpu
                                     or node.gpu_used < node.gpu_alloc)):
                            node.pods.append(pod)
                            node.cpu_used += pod.spec.cpu_milli
                            node.mem_used += pod.spec.mem_mib
                            if pod.spec.needs_gpu:
                                node.gpu_used += 1
                            pod.node = node.name
                            pod.phase = "Running"
                            placed = True
                            break
                    if placed:
                        break
                if not placed:
                    print(f"[sched] pod {pod.spec.name} -> Pending "
                          f"(no node has capacity, CA will scale)")

    def cluster_autoscaler(self):
        """CA watches Pending pods and grows pools to satisfy them."""
        pending = [p for pods in self.deployments.values()
                     for p in pods if p.phase == "Pending"]
        if not pending:
            # Scale-down: remove underused nodes (skip min_nodes)
            for pool in self.pools.values():
                if len(pool.nodes) <= pool.min_nodes:
                    continue
                for node in list(pool.nodes):
                    if node.cpu_used < node.cpu_alloc * 0.15:
                        print(f"[ca] draining underused node {node.name}")
                        pool.nodes.remove(node)
            return
        for pod in pending:
            for pool in self.pools.values():
                if pool.fits(pod.spec) and len(pool.nodes) < pool.max_nodes:
                    pool.provision()
                    break
        self._schedule()

    def status(self):
        for pool in self.pools.values():
            print(f"  pool {pool.name} ({pool.pool_type}): "
                  f"{len(pool.nodes)} nodes")
            for n in pool.nodes:
                print(f"    {n.name}: cpu {n.cpu_used}/{n.cpu_alloc}m "
                      f"mem {n.mem_used}/{n.mem_alloc}MiB pods={len(n.pods)}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    cluster = ManagedCluster("prod-cluster-1", "EKS")
    cluster.add_pool(NodePool("ondemand", "on-demand", 2000, 8192))
    cluster.add_pool(NodePool("spot",     "spot",      4000, 16384))
    cluster.add_pool(NodePool("gpu",      "gpu",       4000, 16384, gpu=1))

    # Burst of API pods beyond current on-demand capacity
    cluster.apply_deployment("api-svc",
        PodSpec("api", "registry.example/api:v2", 500, 512, "on-demand"),
        replicas=12)
    # GPU inference pods
    cluster.apply_deployment("infer",
        PodSpec("inf", "registry.example/inf:v1", 1000, 2048,
                "gpu", needs_gpu=True),
        replicas=4)
    # Background workers on spot
    cluster.apply_deployment("worker",
        PodSpec("wk", "registry.example/wk:v1", 1000, 1024, "spot"),
        replicas=6)

    print("\n-- before CA --")
    cluster.status()
    print("\n-- running CA --")
    cluster.cluster_autoscaler()
    print("\n-- after CA --")
    cluster.status()
```

When the cluster autoscaler provisions a new node, the cloud provider must launch the VM (30–90 seconds on AWS, often 1–3 minutes on cold pools), the node must register with the control plane (5–15 seconds), pull the container image (10–60 seconds depending on size and cache), and then start the Pod.
